album: What We Did on Our Holidays
label: Island Records
description: Sandy Denny's first album with Fairport Convention, cut months after she replaced Judy Dyble, pairs jangly West Coast-style folk-rock with British material like the traditional 'She Moves Through the Fair' and a full-band arrangement of Dylan's 'I'll Keep It with Mine.' Richard Thompson's guitar and Denny's clear, powerful voice start pulling the band away from Byrds worship toward the English ballad tradition. It is the hinge record between Fairport's early American-influenced sound and the folk-rock they would perfect on Liege & Lief.
lineage: Grew out of the same London club and Witchseason-production circuit as Pentangle and Bert Jansch, and set up Unhalfbricking and Liege & Lief, the records that made British trad song a rock instrument.

label: Island Records
description: Released only months before Liege & Lief, Unhalfbricking is the transitional record where Fairport worked out how electric folk-rock should sound: three Bob Dylan covers sit next to Sandy Denny's own 'Who Knows Where the Time Goes?' and the first English-language recording of a Dylan song sung in French, 'Si Tu Dois Partir.' Dave Swarbrick's fiddle, guest on the traditional 'A Sailor's Life,' pushed the band into the modal, drone-heavy sound that became their signature. Drummer Martin Lamble died in the van crash that followed this album's completion, closing the band's first era.
lineage: Bridges Fairport's early American folk-rock covers and the fully traditional Liege & Lief, and 'Who Knows Where the Time Goes?' became one of Sandy Denny's most covered songs across folk and indie circles.
key_tracks: Who Knows Where the Time Goes?

label: Island Records
description: Recorded by a band rebuilding after the crash that killed drummer Martin Lamble, Liege & Lief commits fully to British source material: murder ballads like 'Matty Groves,' the fairy abduction of 'Tam Lin,' and Richard Thompson's own 'Crazy Man Michael' are all played on electric guitar, bass and drums with Dave Swarbrick's fiddle leading the melodies. It is usually cited as the record that invented British electric folk-rock as a genre rather than a novelty. Sandy Denny's voice and Thompson's guitar lines make traditional songs sound like they were written for a rock band.
lineage: Directly followed What We Did on Our Holidays and Unhalfbricking, set the template for Steeleye Span and the whole British folk-rock movement, and is cited by later folk-indebted songwriters up through the Big Thief circle.

label: Island Records
description: Fairport's first album without Sandy Denny, sung mostly by Dave Swarbrick and Simon Nicol, leans harder into instrumental interplay: the nine-minute 'Sloth' builds from a slow ballad into an extended fiddle-and-guitar jam that became a live showcase. 'Sir Patrick Spens' and the closing jig medley keep the traditional-ballad focus of Liege & Lief while the band's sound gets rangier and more improvisational. It is Richard Thompson's last studio album with the group before he went solo.
lineage: Continues the electric-trad sound Liege & Lief established and shows the jam-band side of British folk-rock that later fed jammier folk-adjacent indie acts.

album: The North Star Grassman and the Ravens
label: Island Records
description: Sandy Denny's debut solo album after leaving Fotheringay pairs her own increasingly personal songwriting, especially the elegiac 'Late November' and the war-haunted 'John the Gun,' with covers of Brenda's 'Down in the Flood' and the traditional 'Blackwaterside.' Her old Fairport bandmates and members of Fotheringay back her, so the sound stays close to electric folk-rock even as the album is billed as a solo statement. It set the pattern for her run of solo records through the mid-1970s.
lineage: Follows directly from Fotheringay's breakup and keeps Denny's songwriting in the same Fairport-adjacent folk-rock lineage that later solo albums Sandy and Like an Old Fashioned Waltz continued.

label: Island Records
description: Denny's second solo album is more polished than her Fairport or Fotheringay work, with string and horn arrangements framing 'Listen, Listen' and 'The Lady,' plus a cover of Dylan's 'Tomorrow Is a Long Time.' Her voice carries the record: full, aching, and precise on both her own compositions and the traditional 'Bushes and Briars.' It is generally ranked among her strongest solo statements and a high point of the Island folk-rock roster she came up through.
lineage: Continues the Fairport-and-Fotheringay folk-rock sound in a more orchestrated, singer-songwriter direction that influenced later British female singer-songwriters.

label: Island Records
description: Denny's third solo album pushes further into orchestrated pop and cabaret, with a Cliff Richard duet on 'Whispering Grass' sitting alongside the stark 'At the End of the Day' and 'No End,' one of the bleakest things she recorded. It sold poorly and marked the point where Island's patience with her solo career was running out. The record is less often cited than her Fairport-era work but shows her range past straight folk-rock.
lineage: The least folk-rock of Denny's solo run, pulled toward orchestral pop, though it still follows directly from Sandy and The North Star Grassman and the Ravens.
key_tracks: At the End of the Day

label: Island Records
description: After leaving Fairport Convention, Sandy Denny formed Fotheringay with her partner Trevor Lucas and guitarist Jerry Donahue; their sole album pairs her originals 'Nothing More' and 'The Sea' with a full-band arrangement of Dylan's 'Too Much of Nothing' and the traditional 'Banks of the Nile.' The sound is close to late Fairport but looser and more American-influenced in its guitar interplay. The band broke up before a second album was finished, and Denny went solo shortly after.
lineage: A direct continuation of Denny's Fairport Convention sound with her own band, sitting between Unhalfbricking-era Fairport and her solo albums.

album: I Want to See the Bright Lights Tonight
label: Island Records
description: Richard Thompson's first album after leaving Fairport Convention, recorded on a tight budget with his new wife Linda singing lead on several tracks, is bleaker and more electric than anything in the Fairport catalog: 'The Calvary Cross' and 'Withered and Died' pair his angular guitar lines with grim, plainspoken lyrics. Linda Thompson's voice, clear and slightly weary, gives the duets a different weight than Sandy Denny's Fairport-era singing. It set the template for the duo's decade-long run of albums together.
lineage: Follows Richard Thompson's exit from Fairport Convention and starts the Richard and Linda Thompson partnership that runs through Shoot Out the Lights.
key_tracks: I Want to See the Bright Lights Tonight

label: Island Records
description: A lighter, more music-hall-inflected record than its predecessor, Hokey Pokey mixes seaside-postcard humor on the title track with the tender 'A Heart Needs a Home' and the bitter 'Old Man Inside a Young Man.' Richard Thompson's guitar playing stays sharp even as the arrangements loosen into vaudeville and jug-band touches. It is one of the duo's most purely playful records, released the same year as the much darker Pour Down Like Silver.
lineage: Continues the Richard and Linda Thompson partnership begun on I Want to See the Bright Lights Tonight, folding music-hall humor into the same folk-rock band.
key_tracks: Old Man Inside a Young Man

label: Island Records
description: Recorded soon after the Thompsons converted to Sufi Islam and moved into a religious community, Pour Down Like Silver trades Hokey Pokey's music-hall jokes for devotional, often severe songs like 'Night Comes In' and 'For Shame of Doing Wrong.' The playing is sparer than on the earlier duo records, built around Richard Thompson's guitar and Linda's voice rather than a full band sound. It closes out the pair's mid-1970s run before a several-year gap in their recording career.
lineage: The most explicitly devotional record in the Richard and Linda Thompson catalog, following Hokey Pokey and preceding the long gap before Shoot Out the Lights.

label: Hannibal Records
description: Produced by Joe Boyd and recorded as the Thompsons' marriage was ending, Shoot Out the Lights is a harder, more rock-oriented record than their earlier albums, with Richard Thompson's guitar solos on 'Walking on a Wire' and the title track carrying real menace. Linda Thompson's vocals on songs she didn't know were about their breakup add a documented layer of tension critics have written about for decades. It became the duo's most acclaimed and best-selling album and their last studio record together.
lineage: The later landmark of the Richard and Linda Thompson catalog, closing the folk-rock partnership that began with I Want to See the Bright Lights Tonight and pointing toward Richard Thompson's long solo career.

label: Island Records
description: Richard Thompson's first solo album after leaving Fairport Convention is built entirely from his own songs, mixing accordion and Northumbrian pipes into English folk-rock on 'The New St George' and 'Down Where the Drunkards Roll'-style character sketches like 'Nobody's Wedding.' It sold poorly on release and was famously slagged by an American reviewer, but it has since been reassessed as a key document of Thompson's songwriting voice. Linda Peters, soon to be his wife, sings backing vocals throughout.
lineage: Thompson's first post-Fairport statement, setting up the guitar style and dry, story-driven songwriting he carried into the Richard and Linda Thompson albums.
key_tracks: The Angels Took My Racehorse Away

label: Island Records
description: Nick Drake's debut, produced by Joe Boyd and arranged with Robert Kirby's chamber strings, sets his hushed, intricately fingerpicked guitar and low, unhurried voice against orchestral backing on 'River Man' and 'Way to Blue.' It sold almost nothing on release but has since become one of the most cited records in quiet British songwriting, a direct reference point for hushed indie-folk artists from Elliott Smith to Big Thief's circle. The playing is technically demanding but never shows off; the mood stays melancholy and controlled throughout.
lineage: Emerged from the same Witchseason/Joe Boyd stable as Fairport Convention and John Martyn, and is a foundational reference for the modern indie-folk lineage that runs through Iron & Wine to Big Thief.

label: Island Records
description: Drake's second album adds horns, congas and members of Fairport Convention and John Cale on 'Northern Sky,' pushing his sound toward a breezier, almost jazz-folk pop arrangement without losing the close, intimate guitar work underneath. 'At the Chime of a City Clock' and the instrumental title track show Robert Kirby's arrangements working with the songs rather than around them. It remains the outlier in Drake's catalog, warmer and more outward-facing than Five Leaves Left or Pink Moon.
lineage: The most arranged and outward-looking of Drake's three albums, sitting between the string-laden Five Leaves Left and the stripped-down Pink Moon, and drawing on the same Island/Witchseason session players as Fairport Convention and John Martyn.
key_tracks: At the Chime of a City Clock

label: Island Records
description: Recorded in two late-night sessions with just Drake's voice, guitar and a single piano overdub on the title track, Pink Moon strips away the string arrangements of his first two albums entirely. It is his shortest and starkest record, twenty-eight minutes long, made as his depression deepened; he died two years later. Decades on it is the most widely cited Nick Drake album among indie and indie-folk songwriters, from Adrianne Lenker's Big Thief circle to the freak-folk revival, for its unadorned intimacy.
lineage: The final, most minimal Nick Drake album, and the single most-cited reference point for hushed acoustic indie folk from Elliott Smith through Adrianne Lenker and Big Thief.

label: Transatlantic Records
description: Recorded on a borrowed reel-to-reel in a friend's kitchen and sold to Transatlantic for a flat fee, Bert Jansch's debut announced a new, harder-edged British fingerstyle guitar sound built from folk, blues and jazz phrasing. 'Needle of Death,' a plainspoken song about a friend's heroin overdose, and the instrumental 'Angie' (his arrangement of Davy Graham's tune) became touchstones for a generation of British guitarists including Jimmy Page and Neil Young. The recording is rough and close-miked, which only adds to its intensity.
lineage: Grew out of the Soho folk-club scene alongside Davy Graham and directly shaped Pentangle, Nick Drake's guitar style and the American Primitive/fingerstyle lineage that runs through John Fahey's admirers.

label: Transatlantic Records
description: Recorded with fellow guitarist John Renbourn, Jack Orion turns entirely to traditional balladry, stretching the ten-minute title track and the murder ballad 'Blackwaterside' into extended fingerpicked arrangements that were unusually long and free-form for a folk record at the time. Jansch's guitar playing on 'Blackwaterside' was closely studied (and later disputed) by Jimmy Page for Led Zeppelin's 'Black Mountain Side.' The record is austere, almost droning, with none of the pop concessions of his debut.
lineage: Follows Bert Jansch's 1965 debut deeper into traditional ballad material and directly seeded Pentangle, the duo project he formed with John Renbourn soon after.

label: Charisma Records
description: Made in Los Angeles with former Monkee Michael Nesmith producing, L.A. Turnaround pairs Jansch's fingerstyle guitar with American session players for a sound noticeably warmer and more country-inflected than his Transatlantic-era records, including a re-recorded 'Needle of Death' and the loping 'Fresh as a Sweet Sunday Morning.' It marked Jansch's commercial comeback after Pentangle's breakup and his first album for Charisma. The Nesmith connection ties the British folk guitar tradition directly to the Los Angeles country-rock scene.
lineage: Follows Bert Jansch's solo run and Pentangle years, crossing British fingerstyle folk with the Los Angeles country-rock world via producer Michael Nesmith.
key_tracks: Fresh as a Sweet Sunday Morning
Open Up the Watergate (Let the Sunshine In)

label: Island Records
description: John Martyn's fourth album is the record where his acoustic guitar started taking on the tape-echo and Echoplex treatments that would define his later work, most clearly on the loping 'Head and Heart' and the title track. Danny Thompson's double bass, borrowed from the Pentangle world, gives the songs a loose, jazz-inflected pulse under Martyn's slurred, soulful phrasing. It sits right at the point where British folk guitar starts bending toward jazz and dub.
lineage: Follows Martyn's earlier folk-club albums and points toward Solid Air, carrying the same Danny Thompson/Pentangle-adjacent musicians who linked the London folk and jazz scenes.

label: Island Records
description: Solid Air is John Martyn's best-known record, built around the title track, a slow, vibraphone-tinged elegy written for his friend Nick Drake shortly before Drake's death. 'May You Never' became his most-covered song, and 'Don't Want to Know' shows the Echoplex-treated acoustic guitar sound he had been developing since Bless the Weather. Danny Thompson's double bass and a loose, jazz-club atmosphere separate it from the harder-edged folk-rock of Fairport or Steeleye Span.
lineage: Martyn's peak Island-era record, tied directly to Nick Drake through its title track and continuing the jazz-folk direction begun on Bless the Weather.

label: Transatlantic Records
scene: Horseshoe pub folk club, Tottenham Court Road
description: Pentangle's third album is where the group's fusion of folk song, jazz interplay and blues fully clicked commercially, led by 'Light Flight,' which became a UK top-40 hit and the theme to the TV series Take Three Girls. Bert Jansch and John Renbourn's interlocking guitars, Jacqui McShee's clear soprano and the jazz rhythm section of Danny Thompson and Terry Cox give traditional songs like 'Once I Had a Sweetheart' a loose, swinging feel closer to a jazz combo than a folk group. It is generally considered the band's high point.
lineage: Built from the individual folk-club careers of Bert Jansch and John Renbourn, fusing British folk song with jazz musicianship in a way few contemporaries attempted.

label: CBS Records
description: Unlike Briggs's earlier unaccompanied traditional-song recordings, The Time Has Come is built from her own compositions, sung over her own acoustic guitar and, on one track, Johnny Moynihan's bouzouki. Her plain, unornamented voice and the sparse arrangements make songs like the title track and 'Wishing Well' feel closer to a field recording than a produced folk-rock album. It sold poorly, was dropped from CBS's catalogue soon after, and became a hard-to-find cult record among later British folk revivalists.
lineage: Briggs's traditional unaccompanied singing directly influenced Bert Jansch and Sandy Denny, and this, her most song-based album, sits at the acoustic, least electric edge of the British folk-rock lane.
borderline_note: Very close to unaccompanied source-singing rather than rock; included as the acoustic edge of the lane per the seed list.

label: Decca Records
description: A collaboration between traditional-song singer Shirley Collins and guitar innovator Davy Graham, this album set English and American folk songs like 'Nottamun Town' and 'Reynardine' against Graham's blues- and jazz-inflected fingerstyle guitar, including his own instrumental 'Blue Monk.' Graham's open-tuning, modal approach to the guitar, developed here and on his own records, became foundational for the British fingerstyle players (Jansch, Renbourn, Martyn) who followed him. It predates the main folk-rock era by a few years but is usually cited as the record that made British folk guitar modern.
lineage: A direct root of the British folk-rock and fingerstyle-guitar lineage: Davy Graham's playing here shaped Bert Jansch, John Renbourn and John Martyn, and Collins's song choices fed the repertoire Fairport Convention later electrified.
borderline_note: Released in 1964, a year before this lane's core era begins; kept as the acknowledged root record the rest of the lane's guitarists cite.

label: Philips Records
scene: West Coast Renaissance pilgrimage to the Outer Hebrides
description: Vashti Bunyan wrote these songs on a real horse-and-wagon journey from London toward Donovan's planned commune on Skye, eventually settling on the Hebridean island of Berneray; Joe Boyd produced the finished record with Robert Kirby's gentle string arrangements and guest musicians from Fairport Convention and the Incredible String Band. It sold almost nothing on release and Bunyan left music for three decades, but the album's hushed, lullaby-like songs about the journey, especially 'Diamond Day' and 'Rose Hip November,' were rediscovered around 2000 and became a foundational text for the freak-folk and indie-folk revivals.
lineage: Produced by the same Joe Boyd/Witchseason circle as Nick Drake and Fairport Convention, and its rediscovery directly shaped 2000s freak-folk and the hushed, pastoral strand of indie folk that artists like Devendra Banhart and, later, Big Thief's circle cite.

label: B&C Records
description: Steeleye Span's second album, made after Ashley Hutchings left Fairport Convention to push electric folk further toward unaccompanied traditional song, is harder and starker than Fairport's records: there is no drummer, and Maddy Prior and Martin Carthy's voices carry songs like 'The Blacksmith' and 'False Knight on the Road' over interlocking electric guitars. It is generally considered the most purely 'traditional' of the classic British electric-folk albums, less rock-band than Liege & Lief. The band would soften toward pop with Below the Salt and later hits.
lineage: Formed by ex-Fairport Convention bassist Ashley Hutchings as a harder-line continuation of the Liege & Lief experiment, pushing British trad song even further from rock band conventions.
borderline_note: Borderline for the lane: no drums and closer to unaccompanied trad singing than Fairport's rock-band sound, but included per the assignment as a defining electric-folk record next to Liege & Lief.

label: Dandelion Records
description: John Peel started Dandelion Records specifically to release this album, produced by Peel himself and cut quickly with St John's low, unhurried contralto over her own fingerpicked guitar. The title track and 'Autumn Lullaby' set the tone for a catalogue of plainspoken, unadorned songs that avoided the orchestral flourishes of contemporaries like Nick Drake. St John became one of the few women producers/artists working closely with Peel's label through the early 1970s.
lineage: Part of the same late-1960s London singer-songwriter scene as Nick Drake and John Martyn, distinguished by John Peel's direct patronage through his own Dandelion label.

label: Harvest Records
description: Chapman's second album, cut with a pre-fame Mick Ronson on lead guitar and Rick Kemp (soon of Steeleye Span) on bass, is built around his best-known song, 'Postcards of Scarborough,' a plainspoken portrait of a fading English seaside town. His guitar playing draws on the same fingerstyle vocabulary as Bert Jansch and Davy Graham, but his gravelly, conversational voice and travelogue lyrics push the songs closer to folk-rock storytelling than pure guitar showcase. John Peel championed the record on his radio show, helping it reach UK No. 45.
lineage: Shares session players and a Yorkshire folk-club background with Steeleye Span and the wider Transatlantic/Harvest folk scene, and Chapman's plainspoken storytelling and open-tuned guitar work influenced later British guitarists like Jack Rose's American Primitive circle.

note: Confirmed 1969 release on Harvest Records (SHVL 755, produced by Gus Dudgeon) via Wikipedia artist page, but could not verify the exact track listing from any source actually opened (Wikipedia album page and Discogs release pages returned errors or unrelated content); left out to avoid inventing song titles.
